claim: High levels of TLX correlate with poor patient prognosis in glioblastoma.
source: Interestingly, high levels of the neural stem cell regulator TLX correlate with poor patient prognosis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2010 and Zou et al., 2012 in the introduction section

claim: Tailless initiates tumourigenesis by reverting intermediate neural progenitors to a stem cell state.
source: Here we show that high levels of the Drosophila TLX homologue, Tailless, initiate tumourigenesis by reverting intermediate neural progenitors to a stem cell state.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-5 demonstrating INP to NSC conversion

claim: Asense is a direct target of Tailless.
source: Strikingly, we could block tumour formation completely by re-expressing Asense (homologue of human ASCL1), which we show is a direct target of Tailless.
evidence: Supported by TaDa data showing Tll binding to ase locus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Expression of TLX and ASCL1 are mutually exclusive in glioblastoma.
source: Our results predict that expression of TLX and ASCL1 should be mutually exclusive in glioblastoma, which was verified in single-cell RNA-seq of human glioblastoma samples.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: Counteracting high TLX is a potential therapeutic strategy for suppressing tumours originating from intermediate progenitor cells.
source: Counteracting high TLX is a potential therapeutic strategy for suppressing tumours originating from intermediate progenitor cells.
evidence: Based on inference from rescue experiments showing Ase can block Tll-induced tumours

claim: Tll mRNA is expressed in Type II NSCs but not in their progeny (INPs).
source: We detected tll mRNA in Type II NSCs but not in their progeny (INPs) (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Tll protein is present in NSCs and at low levels in newly-born INPs.
source: while Tll protein was present in NSCs and at low levels in newly-born INPs (Figure 1D–D').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-D'

claim: The DNA binding domains of Tll and TLX are 81% identical (94% similarity).
source: their DNA binding domains are 81% identical (94% similarity)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1E

claim: The ligand binding domains of Tll and TLX are 40% identical (77% similarity).
source: their ligand binding domains are 40% identical (77% similarity)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1E

claim: TLX and Tll bind to the same consensus DNA sequence.
source: In addition, TLX and Tll bind to the same consensus DNA sequence (Yu et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 1994

claim: TLX and Tll recruit conserved cofactors, such as Atrophin, via their ligand binding domains.
source: and recruit conserved cofactors, such as Atrophin, via their ligand binding domains (Wang et al., 2006; Zhi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006 and Zhi et al., 2015

claim: TLX is expressed in NSCs and intermediate progenitor cells in the SVZ of the adult mouse brain.
source: In the SVZ, TLX is detected in NSCs and their progeny, intermediate progenitor cells (Figure 1F; Li et al., 2012; Obernier et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2012 and Obernier et al., 2011, and schematic in Figure 1F

claim: Expressing tll RNAi resulted in the absence of all Type II NSCs.
source: Expressing either tll RNAi construct resulted in the absence of all Type II NSC in all brains assessed (i.e. all NSCs expressed Dpn and Ase) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C'

claim: tll null Type II NSCs underwent a cell fate transition that resulted in the loss of Type II markers.
source: However, we were unable to recover tll null Type II NSC clones, despite mutant clones being visible in other NSC lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). This suggested that tll null Type II NSCs underwent a cell fate transition that resulted in the loss of Type II markers.
evidence: Based on inference from MARCM clone analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F

claim: tll knockdown resulted in derepression of Ase in all Type II NSCs.
source: While Dpn expression was unaffected, tll knockdown resulted in derepression of Ase in all Type II NSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Upon tll knockdown, no INPs could be found in Type II lineages and instead GMCs were positioned adjacent to the NSCs.
source: Strikingly, upon tll knockdown, no INPs (small Dpn+ Ase+) could be found in Type II lineages and instead GMCs (Ase+ Pros+) were positioned adjacent to the NSCs (compare Figure 2A–A'' to Figure 2B-B'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B''

claim: In 6 out of 10 tll knockdown brains, at least one Type II NSC expressed Pros that localised in a crescent at the cell cortex.
source: In 6 out of 10 tll knockdown brains, at least one Type II NSC expressed Pros that localised in a crescent at the cell cortex, indicating asymmetric segregation of Pros to daughter cells (Figure 2B'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B''

claim: Asymmetric segregation of Pros is a feature characteristic of Type I NSCs and INPs that is never observed in Type II NSCs.
source: Asymmetric segregation of Pros is a feature characteristic of Type I NSCs and INPs that is never observed in Type II NSCs (Bayraktar et al., 2010; Bello et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayraktar et al., 2010 and Bello et al., 2008

claim: Expression of Pnt-GFP in Type II NSCs was lost in the absence of tll.
source: Furthermore, expression of Pnt-GFP (Boisclair Lachance et al., 2014) in Type II NSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–C') and the Type II lineage marker, erm-CD4-tdTomato (Han et al., 2011), was lost in the absence of tll (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D

claim: In the absence of tll, Type II NSC lineages are transformed into Type I lineages which exhibit lower neurogenic capacity due to the lack of INPs.
source: We conclude that, in the absence of tll, Type II NSC lineages are transformed into Type I lineages which exhibit lower neurogenic capacity due to the lack of INPs (Figure 2C–C' and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–E').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Tll misexpression in INPs resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of Type II NSCs, from 8 to 109 ± 12.12 per brain lobe.
source: Tll misexpression in INPs resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of Type II NSCs, from 8 to 109 ± 12.12 per brain lobe (Figure 3B–B' and quantified in Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: A strong reduction in the number of differentiating progeny in Type II lineages was observed upon Tll overexpression in INPs.
source: We also observed a strong reduction in the number of differentiating progeny in Type II lineages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D'

claim: Ectopic Tll expression in GMCs or post-mitotic neurons did not generate excess NSCs nor neuronal dedifferentiation.
source: We tested whether Tll expression in more differentiated neural precursors (GMCs) or post-mitotic neurons would also generate excess NSCs but, interestingly, we found that both cell types were resistant to ectopic Tll expression: we observed neither additional NSCs nor neuronal dedifferentiation (Figure 3D–E').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-E'

claim: Ectopic Tll expression in Type II lineages promotes NSC fate at the expense of self-renewing cells, specifically INPs.
source: Therefore, ectopic Tll expression in Type II lineages promotes NSC fate at the expense of self-renewing cells, specifically INPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–E').
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Expressing Tll throughout the CNS resulted in large tumour-like growths in the adult brain that consisted almost entirely of NSCs.
source: When we expressed Tll throughout the CNS, we observed large tumour-like growths in the adult brain that consisted almost entirely of NSCs (Dpn+ cells) (compare Figure 4A–A').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-A'

claim: High levels of Tll resulted in Dpn+ NSCs in both the central brain and ventral nerve cord at larval stages.
source: At larval stages, we found that high levels of Tll resulted in Dpn+ NSCs in both the central brain and ventral nerve cord, indicating that ectopic Tll can induce tumours from Type I NSCs (Figure 4B–B').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-B'

claim: Tll-induced tumours in the ventral nerve cord consisted almost entirely of NSCs that were negative for Ase, indicating a Type II-like NSC fate.
source: Remarkably, Tll-induced tumours consisted almost entirely of NSCs that were negative for Ase, indicating a Type II-like NSC fate (Figure 4C–C').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-C'

claim: The tumour NSCs lacked Pros, consistent with a change in identity to Type II NSC.
source: Consistent with a change in identity to Type II NSC, the tumour NSCs lacked Pros (Figure 4D–D'; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-D' and citation to Bayraktar et al., 2010

claim: A subset of transformed Type I NSCs generated INPs.
source: Furthermore, a subset of these transformed Type I NSCs generated INPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–A'), indicating that Tll is sufficient to induce a switch in NSC identity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-A'

claim: The appearance of ectopic Type II-like NSCs was associated with a reduction in GMCs and neurons.
source: The appearance of the ectopic Type II-like NSCs (Dpn+ Ase-) was associated with a reduction in GMCs and neurons, as assessed by expression of Pros (Figure 4D–D').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-D'

claim: Expressing Tll in Type I lineages directs a change in NSC identity and blocks differentiation, resulting in large NSC tumours comprised of Type II NSCs.
source: We conclude that expressing Tll in Type I lineages not only directs a change in NSC identity but also blocks differentiation in these newly transformed lineages, resulting in large NSC tumours comprised of Type II NSCs (Figure 4E–E').
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Expressing high levels of Tll in INPs resulted in supernumerary Type II NSCs, which had previously expressed erm-GAL4 but lacked current expression.
source: Expressing high levels of Tll in INPs resulted in supernumerary Type II NSCs, which had previously expressed erm-GAL4 but lacked current expression (Figure 5A' and quantified in Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by G-TRACE data shown in Figure 5A' and 5B

claim: Tll expression is sufficient to induce a cell fate change from INP to NSC.
source: We conclude that Tll expression is sufficient to induce a cell fate change from INP to NSC and our results implicate INP reversion to NSCs as the mechanism of tumour initiation.
evidence: Based on inference from G-TRACE data shown in Figure 5

claim: Human TLX can initiate tumours from INPs via similar regulatory pathways as Drosophila Tll.
source: To investigate whether human TLX could also initiate tumours from INPs via similar regulatory pathways, we expressed TLX in combination with G-TRACE in INPs. As for Tll, we observed ectopic Type II NSCs with historic erm-GAL4 expression only (Figure 5A'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A''

claim: Both Tll and TLX can initiate tumourigenesis from neural lineages by reverting INPs to NSCs.
source: Our results indicate that both Tll and TLX can initiate tumourigenesis from neural lineages by reverting INPs to NSCs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Neither TLX nor Tll could revert post-mitotic neurons to NSCs.
source: Interestingly, neither TLX nor Tll could revert post-mitotic neurons to NSCs, demonstrating that neurons are resistant to tumour initiation (see Figure 3D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: INPs represent a tumour-susceptible cell type and are the tumour cells of origin for TLX- and Tll-induced tumours in Drosophila.
source: We conclude that INPs represent a tumour-susceptible cell type and are the tumour cells of origin for TLX- and Tll-induced tumours in Drosophila (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Tll binds to the ase locus in Type II NSCs.
source: We profiled Tll binding in Type II NSCs (16 per brain; approximately 700 NSCs per replicate) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B) and identified Tll-binding peaks at 2495 protein-coding genes (see 'Tll TaDa binding targets.xlsx' for full list of Tll targets), including ase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by TaDa data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Tll binds ase directly and represses its expression to promote Type II NSC fate.
source: We conclude that Tll binds ase directly and represses its expression to promote Type II NSC fate.
evidence: Based on inference from TaDa data and expression analysis

claim: The loss of Ase alone is not sufficient to induce Type II fate in Type I NSCs.
source: However, the loss of Ase alone is not sufficient to induce Type II fate in Type I NSCs (Bowman et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowman et al., 2008

claim: Tll acts on additional target genes beyond ase to mediate cell fate change and tumour initiation.
source: indicating that Tll acts on additional target genes to mediate this cell fate change and tumour initiation.
evidence: Based on inference from the fact that Ase loss alone is not sufficient

claim: Pros is bound by Tll in Type II NSCs.
source: One potential candidate is Pros, which we found was also bound by Tll in Type II NSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by TaDa data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: Pros is known to negatively regulate NSC proliferation.
source: Pros is known to negatively regulate NSC proliferation (Cabernard and Doe, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cabernard and Doe, 2009

claim: Pros is repressed when Tll is expressed at high levels.
source: and is also repressed when Tll is expressed at high levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–C' and Figure 4D–D'; Kurusu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-C' and Figure 4D-D', and citation to Kurusu et al., 2009

claim: Expressing Ase together with Tll completely abolished tumourigenesis in all brains analysed.
source: We expressed Ase together with Tll and found, remarkably, that tumourigenesis was completely abolished in all brains analysed (n = 10) (Figure 6A–A'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-A''

claim: Ase prevented the production of ectopic NSCs and re-established normal neurogenesis in Type I NSC lineages.
source: Strikingly, not only did Ase prevent the production of ectopic NSCs, it also re-established normal neurogenesis in Type I NSC lineages: the production of GMCs and neurons was restored, as revealed by expression of Pros and Elav (Figure 6A–A'' and B–B'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B''

claim: Re-introducing Ase into Tll tumours did not repress the expression of Tll.
source: However, re-introducing Ase into Tll tumours did not repress the expression of Tll (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–A'')
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-A''

claim: Ectopic expression of Ase does not turn off Tll in Type II NSCs.
source: nor does the ectopic expression of Ase turn off Tll in Type II NSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–B').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-B'

claim: Expressing Ase reinstates the normal neurogenic programme and prevents tumour initiation by Tll.
source: Therefore, by expressing Ase we were able to reinstate the normal neurogenic programme and prevent tumour initiation by Tll (Figure 6C–C'').
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: High TLX expression is correlated with poor patient prognosis in human glioblastoma.
source: In human glioblastoma, high TLX expression is correlated with poor patient prognosis (Park et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2010 and Zou et al., 2012

claim: Low ASCL1 levels are correlated with shorter survival time in glioblastoma.
source: Intriguingly, ASCL1 levels also vary between human glioblastoma samples and low levels are correlated with shorter survival time (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2017

claim: Increasing ASCL1 levels promotes terminal differentiation and attenuates tumorigenicity.
source: Increasing ASCL1 levels was shown to promote terminal differentiation and attenuate tumorigenicity.
evidence: Based on inference from Park et al., 2017 study mentioned in context

claim: Expression of both TLX and ASCL1 is restricted to malignant glioblastoma cells.
source: Our analysis identified 7,835 single cells in this data set and, following cluster annotation based on previously known markers (Neftel et al., 2019), we found that expression of both TLX and ASCL1 was restricted to the malignant glioblastoma cells (6,766 cells) (Figure 7A–A').
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A-A'

claim: Very few malignant glioblastoma cells expressed both TLX and ASCL1 transcripts.
source: However, when we compared TLX and ASCL1 expression within the malignant population, we found very few cells that expressed both transcripts (Figure 7B), suggesting that TLX and ASCL1 are indeed mutually exclusive in malignant glioblastoma cells.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: Tll is expressed in Type II NSCs during larval development, where it is required for Type II NSC identity and subsequent lineage progression.
source: We showed that Tll is expressed in Type II NSCs during larval development, where it is required for Type II NSC identity and subsequent lineage progression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: In the absence of Tll, the proneural transcription factor Ase is derepressed in Type II NSCs.
source: In the absence of Tll, the proneural transcription factor Ase is derepressed in Type II NSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Transit amplifying INPs are no longer generated in the absence of Tll, and the resulting NSC lineages have a lower neurogenic potential.
source: As a consequence, transit amplifying INPs are no longer generated and the resulting NSC lineages have a lower neurogenic potential.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: High levels of TLX in human glioblastoma are correlated with tumour aggressiveness.
source: High levels of TLX in human glioblastoma are correlated with tumour aggressiveness (Park et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2010 and Zou et al., 2012

claim: High level expression of TLX results in glioblastoma-like lesions derived from SVZ NSC lineages in mouse models.
source: High level expression of TLX results in glioblastoma-like lesions derived from SVZ NSC lineages in mouse models of glioblastoma (Liu et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2010

claim: TLX and Drosophila Tll are highly conserved proteins.
source: TLX and its Drosophila homologue, Tll, are highly conserved proteins (Yu et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 1994

claim: Both TLX and Tll are able to revert INPs to NSC fate as a first step in tumour initiation.
source: and we found that both genes are able to revert INPs to NSC fate as a first step in tumour initiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Ectopic expression of Tll was sufficient to induce the expansion of NSCs throughout the Drosophila CNS.
source: Ectopic expression of Tll was also sufficient to induce the expansion of NSCs throughout the Drosophila CNS, demonstrating the widespread vulnerability of NSC and progenitor populations to ectopic Tll expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: The ectopic NSCs resulting from high Tll expression are negative for Ase.
source: We found that the ectopic NSCs resulting from high Tll expression are negative for Ase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: The absence of Ase is a hallmark of Type II NSCs.
source: The absence of Ase is a hallmark of Type II NSCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Type II NSC markers

claim: Ectopic Tll promotes a cell fate change from INP/Type I NSC to Type II NSC and thereby initiates tumourigenesis.
source: Therefore, ectopic Tll promotes a cell fate change from INP/Type I NSC to Type II NSC and thereby initiates tumourigenesis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 3-5

claim: The capacity of Tll to induce NSC expansion had been reported previously as part of a study on mushroom body NSCs and GMCs.
source: The capacity of Tll to induce NSC expansion had been reported previously as part of a study showing that Tll regulates the proliferation of larval mushroom body NSCs and GMCs (Kurusu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurusu et al., 2009

claim: Tll-induced tumourigenesis could be blocked by ectopic expression of Pros.
source: Tll-induced tumourigenesis could be blocked by ectopic expression of Pros (Kurusu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurusu et al., 2009

claim: Ectopic Pros results in the loss of NSCs even in wild type brains.
source: However, ectopic Pros results in the loss of NSCs even in wild type brains (Cabernard and Doe, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cabernard and Doe, 2009

claim: Type I NSC lineages appear normal after Ase misexpression in wild type brains.
source: In contrast, Type I NSC lineages appear normal after Ase misexpression in wild type brains (Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowman et al., 2008

claim: High levels of PROX1 exacerbate glioblastoma.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that high levels of the human homologue of Pros, PROX1, exacerbate glioblastoma (Elsir et al., 2010; Goudarzi et al., 2018; Roodakker et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Elsir et al., 2010; Goudarzi et al., 2018; Roodakker et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017

claim: The tumourigenic capacity of Drosophila Tll and human TLX is highly conserved.
source: We found that the tumourigenic capacity of Drosophila Tll and human TLX was highly conserved (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Human TLX can induce ectopic Type II NSCs from INPs through the repression of Ase.
source: Human TLX could also induce ectopic Type II NSCs from INPs through the repression of Ase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The origin of human glioblastoma has been mapped to the SVZ.
source: It is notable that the origin of human glioblastoma has been mapped to the SVZ (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2018

claim: TLX positive NSCs have been identified in both the SVZ and dentate gyrus.
source: While TLX positive NSCs have been identified in both the SVZ and dentate gyrus, high levels of TLX giving rise to glioblastoma has only been shown robustly in the SVZ (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2010

claim: Low expression levels of ASCL1 correlate with glioblastoma malignancy.
source: Furthermore, a recent study demonstrated that low expression levels of ASCL1 correlate with glioblastoma malignancy (Park et al., 2017).

claim: Ectopic expression of ASCL1 in glioblastoma stem cells was sufficient to promote neuronal differentiation.
source: Ectopic expression of ASCL1 in glioblastoma stem cells was sufficient to promote neuronal differentiation.

claim: Introducing ASCL1 would override the repressive effect of TLX, induce neuronal differentiation and reduce tumour growth.
source: Based on our results in Drosophila, we predict that introducing ASCL1 would override the repressive effect of TLX, induce neuronal differentiation and reduce tumour growth, thereby providing an effective treatment.
evidence: Based on speculation from Drosophila results

claim: INPs are the tumour initiating cells in Type II NSC lineages expressing high levels of Tll.
source: Our results indicate that INPs are the tumour initiating cells in Type II NSC lineages expressing high levels of the orphan nuclear receptor Tll
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Intermediate progenitors are potentially implicated as one of the cells of origin in TLX+ glioblastomas.
source: and potentially implicate intermediate progenitors as one of the cells of origin in TLX+ glioblastomas, an aggressive and lethal brain tumour.
evidence: Based on speculation from Drosophila results

claim: Ase is a direct target of Tll.
source: We found that Ase is a direct target of Tll
evidence: Supported by TaDa data showing Tll binding to ase locus

claim: Ase expression blocks Tll-induced tumourigenesis and reinstates a normal neural differentiation programme.
source: and that Ase expression not only blocks Tll-induced tumourigenesis, but also reinstates a normal neural differentiation programme.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: TLX is expressed in adult NSCs, where it is required for neurogenesis in both the subventricular zone (SVZ) and the subgranular zone (SGZ).
source: TLX is expressed in adult NSCs, where it is required for neurogenesis in both the subventricular zone (SVZ) and the subgranular zone (SGZ) (Liu et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2008; Zou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2008; Zou et al., 2012

claim: TLX is expressed in glioblastoma stem cells.
source: TLX is also expressed in glioblastoma stem cells (Zhu et al., 2014)

claim: Upregulation of TLX promotes gliomagenesis in the mouse SVZ.
source: and upregulation of TLX promotes gliomagenesis in the mouse SVZ (Liu et al., 2010).

claim: TLX is an important stem cell regulator both in normal and tumourigenic conditions.
source: These results indicate that TLX is an important stem cell regulator both in normal and tumourigenic conditions.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies

claim: Astrocyte-like neural stem cells (NSCs) in the SVZ of glioblastoma patients harbour driver mutations that are found in the patient's tumour.
source: A recent study revealed that astrocyte-like neural stem cells (NSCs) in the SVZ of glioblastoma patients harbour driver mutations that are found in the patient's tumour, suggesting that astrocyte-like NSCs are cells of origin of glioblastoma in humans (Lee et al., 2018).

claim: Neural lineages become more resistant to glioblastoma transformation as differentiation progresses.
source: Neural lineages become more resistant to glioblastoma transformation as differentiation progresses, supporting stem cells or early progenitor cells as a common source of glioblastoma (Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2019

claim: Both stem and progenitor cells express Nestin.
source: For example, both stem and progenitor cells express Nestin (Chen et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009

claim: GFAP labels both stem cells and astrocytes.
source: and GFAP labels both stem cells and astrocytes (Doetsch et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doetsch et al., 1999

claim: TLX is expressed in NSCs during embryonic development and in adulthood in mice.
source: In mice, TLX is expressed in NSCs during embryonic development and in adulthood (Li et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2004

claim: Embryonic NSCs display defects in proliferation in the absence of TLX.
source: Embryonic NSCs display defects in proliferation in the absence of TLX (Li et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2008

claim: The loss of TLX in adults results in the loss of transit-amplifying intermediates and reduction in neurogenesis.
source: and the loss of TLX in adults results in the loss of transit-amplifying intermediates and reduction in neurogenesis (Li et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2008; Niu et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2008; Niu et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2004

claim: A cell fate change may occur due to the loss of TLX in mouse NSCs.
source: While these effects were previously attributed to changes in the NSC cell cycle, our results suggest a cell fate change may occur due to the loss of TLX.

claim: Tll was expressed in Type II NSCs throughout larval development.
source: We found that Tll was expressed in Type II NSCs throughout larval development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).

source: while Tll protein was present in NSCs and at low levels in newly-born INPs (Figure 1D–D').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-D'

claim: Mature INPs do not express Tll.
source: Mature INPs (small Dpn+ cells in the lineage) do not express Tll.

source: Tll-GFP (green) is expressed in Type II NSCs (Dpn+ (red) and Ase- (blue)) (arrowheads and outlined with solid white lines) and downregulated in differentiating lineages (dotted white lines) during larval development.
